items.title: 1991 Had More Great Movies Than You Remember: 10 Overlooked Gems
items.summary: 1991 was a huge year for movies, so it makes sense that there are a lot of overlooked titles left on the table. Who could pay attention to every movie coming out in between all-timer titles like The Silence of the Lambs, Beauty and the Beast, Boyz n the Hood, Terminator 2: Judgment Day, Home Alone, and Thelma & Louise? We’re only human. We simply don’t have the bandwidth. However, as these movies all celebrate their 35th anniversary, let’s take a look at 10 underappreciated 1991 gems that deserve more attention. 10. Sleeping with the Enemy This Julia Roberts thriller is the lowest on the list because it was actually a huge hit in 1991, ultimately becoming the seventh highest-grossing movie at the domestic box office that year. However, over time, it has been overshadowed by the other 1990s Julia Roberts classics that came both before (Pretty Woman) and after it (My Best Friend’s Wedding, Runaway Bride, Notting Hill, 2000’s Erin Brockovich). Regardless of its reputation relative to her overall filmography, Sleeping with the Enemy is a winner, blending small town romance with slasher-thriller tropes in a delicious way that many a Lifetime movie has tried to replicate over the years. 9. The People Under the Stairs The People Under the Stairs is a Wes Craven classic that deserves to be on the Mount Rushmore of his filmography alongside A Nightmare on Elm Street, Scream, and The Last House on the Left. In addition to boasting trenchant subtext about white landlords abusing tenants of color, the movie is a wild thrill ride that features two exquisitely twisted villain performances from Twin Peaks alumni Wendy Robie and Everett McGill. 8. Poison Poison, which is the debut feature of Todd Haynes (Carol, May December), interweaves three stories adapted from Jean Genet novels. items.title: Why the 'Nimrods' Score Needed to Get Out of Green Day’s Way
items.summary: Alec Puro has scored zombie thrillers, sitcoms, animated kids' shows, indie horror, and indie drama. He also founded Viralnoise, a royalty-free music platform for content creators. This month, he adds a Green Day-inspired road comedy to his slate. Nimrods, out August 14, follows three teenage bandmates who steal a taxi and drive from Kansas City to Los Angeles, convinced they've been booked to open for Green Day on New Year's Eve. Writer/director Lee Kirk developed the story with Billie Joe Armstrong, Mike Dirnt, and Tré Cool. The band is threaded through every layer of the film, from cameos to a 30-track soundtrack featuring 22 career-spanning Green Day cuts and four unreleased live recordings from a Palladium show captured during the making of the film. Puro's original score has to live inside that framework (he's also scored Lila McLaughlin's Don't Let Them Out, out the same day, and Joseph Hahn's Linkin Park doc Unshatter, due later this year). We spoke with him via Zoom ahead of the film’s release to talk about his work, and to pull out what you can steal from his experience the next time you're working with a composer of your own. - YouTube www.youtube.com You Can Bring Your Composer In Early Puro said Kirk pulled him into the project long before there was a picture to score to. Kirk and the band had been developing the story for a while, he said, and Puro spent months in conversation with Kirk about what the movie was, what it wanted to feel like, and where music might live in it. He watched a rough cut much later. Puro said he especially likes collaborating with bands (he came up as the drummer for the rock band Deadsy). “It's a team sport, which I love.” A composer can come in at many different points of a production. They might see a script, or they might be delivered a final product. items.title: How Indie Filmmakers Can Turn Production Limitations Into Creative Opportunities
items.summary: Independent filmmaking often means making decisions around time constraints, budget, equipment, and resources. But those decisions also come with important lessons about filmmaking in general and creative solutions that make you better at your craft. For The Veil Chapter One: Roadkill, the first installment of Brooke Becker and Delaney Sharpe’s new horror anthology series, the filmmakers faced a number of challenges, including a significant electrical setback that cost them 90 minutes of an already tight eight-hour shoot. Sharpe says, “We learned that resourcefulness isn’t just about solving problems when they arise; it can actually become part of the creative process, forcing you to think differently about how you build tension, environment, and scares.” In this conversation with No Film School, Becker and Sharpe discuss everything from drawing inspiration from The Haunting of Hill House to navigating challenges on an indie set, including rethinking coverage and shooting setups, incorporating unexpected drone footage, and using practical lighting and post-production techniques to maximize their resources. Let's dive in. - YouTubewww.youtube.com NFS: Both, What first sparked the idea for The Veil Chapter One: Roadkill, and what made it the right project to launch Black Ribbon Productions? Brooke Becker: For this series, I took inspiration from vintage paperback scary story anthologies; the kind I used to get at the Scholastic Book Fair for five dollars and read under the covers at night until I got too scared to sleep. The Veil was developed as an ongoing horror anthology series for YouTube from the beginning, so we wanted to optimize it for the platform by parceling out each story to be a bite-sized watch, leaving you wanting more. Delaney Sharpe: Brooke and I had been working on pre-production for the first two chapters of The Veil, and at the time, Roadkill was actually slotted to be the second installment. items.title: What We Can Learn from These Dark Comedies
items.summary: Sometimes, you're not in the mood for rainbows and cotton candy. You need something with a bit more edge, for whatever reason. There are times as a movie viewer (or human being) that you don't feel like sunshine and want comedy with a bite. Enter the dark comedy. It's a genre I love, and it's also one of the most risky, razor-thin tones to hit as a writer and/or director. The humor still has to hit, but it almost feels like a punch to the gut at the same time, like you aren't sure if you have permission to laugh. The drama behind the bits is often heavy, but the levity gives you just enough room. And, heck, I'm in the mood for that this week. Here are five of our favorites that walked the line perfectly, and what the filmmakers said about that. - YouTube www.youtube.com Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb Is there an easier example than Dr. Strangelove? The kooky, madcap drama of a world on the brink of nuclear disaster shouldn't work as well as it does, but the fact that every character buys into the high drama and ridiculous reasoning of the story (and that you have Peter Sellers in multiple roles) makes this a blast. Pun intended. Stanley Kubrick adapted the thriller from Peter George's Red Alert. He realized there was an inherent absurdism in the narrative that couldn't be avoided. "During the past six years," Kubrick told Terry Southern (via Filmmaker Magazine), "I've read almost every available book on the nuclear situation, including regular issues of Air Force Magazine, Missiles and Rockets, Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists and so on. What has struck me is their cautious sterility of ideas, the reverence of obsolete national goals, the breeziness of crackpot realism, the paradox of nuclear threatsmanship, the desperately utopian wish fantasies about Soviet intentions, and the terrifying logic of paranoiac fears and suspicions. items.title: Film Quote of the Day: 'The Godfather Part: III' Quote That Revealed Don Corleone's Philosophy
items.summary: It's safe to say that The Godfather trilogy is one of the greatest of all time. It covers the Corleone family from their time in Italy to America and then back to Italy once again. There are whole lives, a lot of death, and it plays out like a tragedy. All this is wound into three distinct mafia movies. Francis Ford Coppola and Mario Puzo built the trilogy around the friction between personal loyalty and ruthless capitalism. And each movie takes on a different timeline to show how that stays true the whole time. There are so many great lines across all the movies that I want to give a little attention to the third film, which gets maligned and unfairly juxtaposed against the other two. Within, there's a philosophical discussion that I think echoes all the lessons Michael Corleone has learned across the films. So today, we're going to unpack that Godfather: Part III quote and what it means. Let's dive in. - YouTube www.youtube.com The Scene in Question The third movie follows the same sort of mold as the other two, opening on a party where we're caught up on all the family drama and then unfolding the fallout. Like the other iterations, we see the plan to make more money for the family and to expand their empire. We follow an aging Don Michael Corleone who attempts to legitimize himself and move completely away from the mafia by pouring massive capital into Vatican-controlled real estate, which effectively cleans all his money. Michael has a meeting with Archbishop Gilday, who reveals that the Church's financial arm has racked up astronomical deficits through corrupt deals and misplaced trust. And all this happened because he trusted his friend, and he got betrayed. Now, Archbishop Gilday needs a bailout from Michael Corleone. Gilday attempts to gloss over the catastrophe with platitudes about faith and life, but Michael cuts through that. In many ways, he's a much smarter mafia boss than the church. items.title: Remember That Time Chuck Norris Stopped a Chainsaw With His Bare Hands?
items.summary: The world lost an action movie titan when Chuck Norris passed away earlier this year. And while he may be gone, he’s certainly not forgotten. One of the biggest stars of the 80s and 90s “ultimate” era of action movies, Norris was a familiar name alongside other box-office marquee regulars like Arnold, Stallone, Willis, and Van Damme. Yet, while all of these action stars were larger than life in their own ways, Chuck Norris has a legacy that took on a life of its own and surpassed even the greatest, most impressive, and heroic feats of his peers. Thanks in part to Conan O’Brien, Walker, Texas Ranger levers and online jokes, many of these throwaway moments from Norris’ filmography became some of the most iconic memes in film history. And today we honor one of the greatest ones of them all from Forest Warrior (1996). Looking Back at ‘Forest Warrior’ (1996) Released in 1996 as a direct-to-video title directed by Chuck Norris’ brother Aaron, who actually had a pretty prolific action career in his own right, serving as a stunt performer and director in many of Chuck’s films and television shows over their careers, Forest Warrior might have been the final nail in the coffin in Chuck’s marquee action movie career. Released the same year as the first episode of Walker, Texas Ranger, Chuck and his crew were about to make the successful transition from action movies to the safe confines of family-drama television, as Walker would go on to be a primetime mainstay on CBS for nearly a decade. Yet, when filmed, Forest Warrior was always going to be a low-budget, DTV-style project cashing in on Chuck’s star power one more time, even as audiences were beginning to be ready to move on from the over-the-top action style of the 80s and early 90s. Chuck Norris as Jebediah McKenna Chuck Norris plays Jebediah McKenna, a frontiersman killed a century ago, who is magically brought back to life to protect the forest he loved.
